"They are very large and clumsy," I replied.

"Do you think that it would be possible for a large man to get
through that window?"

I examined it carefully, and I found that the wooden bars were
too strong and closely spaced for anyone to pass through, though
there was a certain amount of space between the frames which might
possibly afford a small person a slender opportunity of passage.

"What do you think, Miss Stoner?" asked Holmes.

"Impossible. I think that I am now convinced that I did hear the
whistle, and also the metallic clang. But how could anyone get
out?"

"That is the problem which we have to solve," Holmes remarked.

"If there is nothing else, we may return to our examination."
"By all means."
We went into the room, and Miss Stoner went over to the bed.  "That is my sister's bed," said she.  "It has not been slept in since her death."  Holmes drew a chair up to the bed and carefully examined the whole of its framework.  He ran his hand under the edge and felt along the seam.

"Well?" said I, when he had made his scrutiny.

"The bed is as old as the house," said he. "There is the original
tester, the very ropes which held the canopy. It has been used
for the purposes of a bed for about two hundred years. But it is
in the lower bed that the mystery lies."

"But there is nothing strange about it."

"Not if you are satisfied with the obvious. But what are those
marks?"  He pointed to two small round holes on the wooden frame
near the head of the bed.

"I cannot tell you, but I never noticed them before."

"You are quick-witted, Miss Stoner. See here. Does that suggest
anything to you?" He brought his lens up to the hole.

"It looks as if something had been twisted there."

"So it has. They have driven something through that wood.
There is a faint marking here which shows where the object has
been driven in."

We passed into the room, and Holmes instantly examined the floor,
walls, and ceiling with the keenest attention. "This is a very
ancient building," he remarked. "It is built of a kind of
granite which is very common in this neighbourhood. The method
of construction is most peculiar. The stones are extremely large,
and the joints are very irregular, some being quite a foot or more
in breadth."

"Yes, I noticed that yesterday."

"And look at these windows," he continued. "They are not
casements, but are solid granite blocks fitted into the masonry.
Well, then, this peculiar granite is not found anywhere else in
the country, and these old-fashioned windows are very rarely met
with now. Thus we see that the house has been built of stones
which have been taken from some other building, and that this
building was of very ancient date."

"But this does not help us in the case."

"Ah, my dear Miss Stoner, you will find that it does. Your
stepfather, you say, has an extraordinary knowledge of Indian
animals. He has given lectures upon the subject before now,
hasn't he?"

"Oh yes, and his lectures were very impressive. He has quite a
museum in his study."

"And is he well informed on the subject of the deadly
creatures of the Indian jungle? He knows the habits of snakes,
I suppose?"

"I am sure that he does."

"And you are aware that the Indian snake charmers have a
peculiar method of mesmerizing their snakes? By the way, do you
know what is the main ingredient in their snake-charming
mixture?"

"It is a very difficult question, Mr. Holmes, for I am not sure
that I could put my finger upon it."

"The key of the whole mystery," said Holmes, "lies in those
Indian animals. I wish that I had not left my lens downstairs, for
I could show you some strange things in that room. You have not
seen these things, Miss Stoner? I expect that they will tell us
something of interest."

We passed next into the chamber of the unfortunate Julia, and here
Holmes’s powers of observation were exercised to their utmost.
With his long, thin fingers he examined the walls with the keenest
attention, and then, with his lens, very carefully scrutinized the
floor, while Miss Stoner stood by, her face pale with an
expectant interest.

"What is that?" she asked suddenly.

"It appears to be a single mark," Holmes replied; "and here is
another. They look like the traces of very small feet. What
might they be?"

"Oh, I do not know," she answered; "it is all so mysterious. If
only you could throw some light on this dreadful affair!"
A small side door led into the whitewashed corridor from which
the three bedrooms opened. Holmes refused to examine the third
chamber, so we passed at once to the second, that in which Miss
Stoner was now sleeping, and in which her sister had met with her
fate. It was a homely little room, with a low ceiling and a
gaping fireplace, after the fashion of old country-houses. A
brown chest of drawers stood in one corner, a narrow
white-counterpaned bed in another, and a dressing-table on the
left-hand side of the window. These articles, with two small
wicker-work chairs, made up all the furniture in the room save
for a square of Wilton carpet in the centre. The boards round and
the panelling of the walls were of brown, worm-eaten oak, so old
and discoloured that it may have dated from the original building
of the house. Holmes drew one of the chairs into a corner and sat
silent, while his eyes travelled round and round and up and down,
taking in every detail of the apartment.

"Where does that bell communicate with?" he asked at last
pointing to a thick bell-rope which hung down beside the bed, the
tassel actually lying upon the pillow.

"It goes to the housekeeper's room."

"It looks newer than the other things?"

"Yes, it was only put there a couple of years ago."

"Your sister asked for it, I suppose?"

"No, I never heard of her using it. We used always to get what we
wanted for ourselves."

"I don't know that I am very much surprised," remarked Holmes.
"Indeed, I think that I am beginning to understand this matter
rather better now. Let us go into your room and see if we can find
out the cause of this ingenious device."

"There are only two things in this room to which I could direct
your particular attention," said Miss Stoner, as we followed her
into the adjoining chamber. "This chest of drawers has always
been rather troublesome, it sticks terribly, and it is very difficult
to open it."

"Indeed," said Holmes, "and it is fastened on the inside.
That is certainly rather peculiar, since it is quite unnecessary.
Now let us open the window and get a good view of the lawn."

"And very useful too. From the way that the hook is placed it is
evident that this bell was used, not to summon the house-keeper,
but to warn the person in the next room when anyone was coming
along the passage."

"Why should anyone want to give such a warning?"

"Ah, that is the question which we must answer. But before we
go I want to examine the ventilator."

"Exactly. And there is the end of this little mystery. You can
see now that the only possible way of reaching this room is
through the door. We are now only concerned with explaining how
a woman was murdered, or terrified to death, in a room which
was closed on the inside, and which could not have been entered
from the outside. And now I think we shall understand." He
examined the ventilator, and suddenly bent down and peered
into the opening. "Have you got a dark lantern?" he asked.

"I have one here."

"Good, now we shall get down to the root of the matter."

"Exactly. And you did not notice that the ventilator is much
larger than is usual?" He measured it with his tape.  "Four
inches -- that is somewhat unusual in an old house.  What is this
above the bed?"

He pointed to a small, dark stain upon the whitewashed wall above
the head of the bed.

"I have not seen it before," said Miss Stoner.  "It is not
there in the daytime."

"It has only been placed there recently.  It is clearly of recent
origin."

"Very strange," muttered Holmes, "very strange. The only possible
explanation I can think of is that it was placed there by your
stepfather to mislead the police in case he should commit some
crime in this room."

"What, then, is the meaning of it all?"

"We are now sufficiently familiar with the room," said Holmes.
"Let us go into the next one."

"My bedroom?"

"Yes, your bedroom, I am quite sure of it. But before we go,
Miss Stoner, let me ask you one more question. Was there anything
peculiar about your sister's death which struck you at the time
or which you have recalled since?"

Miss Stoner shook her head sadly.

"There was nothing unusual except that when she was quite unconscious, and as she lay on the bed, I saw my sister make one
final effort to point in the direction of my stepfather’s
room. But it was too late, and her words were lost. She was
already dead."

"Would you mind raising the blind, Miss Stoner?"

"The light is very strong, Mr Holmes."

"Please raise it all the same."

"Very strange!" muttered Holmes, pulling at the rope. "There are
one or two very singular points about this room. For example,
what a fool a builder must be to open a ventilator into another
room, when, with the same trouble, he might have communicated
with the outside air!"

"That is also quite modern," said the lady.

"Done about the same time as the bell-rope?" remarked Holmes.

"Yes, there were several little changes carried out about that
time."

Dr. Roylott's chamber was larger than that of his stepdaughters,
but was as plainly furnished. A camp-bed, a small wooden table,
and a couple of chairs were the only things in it. In one corner
stood a tall, dark, narrow cupboard. The atmosphere was close and
heavy, and the smell of strong Indian cigars was overpowering.
Holmes sniffed at it with his characteristic avidity. "Tobacco,
my dear Watson," said he; "most excellent tobacco! This is a
very distinguished cigar indeed, one that is not often met with
outside of Havana. There are, however, one or two points about
the room which are of interest."

He walked over to the cupboard and examined the lock with great
attention. "This must be a very ancient lock," said he.
"It's a peculiar mechanism."

"I have never known him to use a key," said Miss Stoner.
"He always keeps it closed."

"I see. And this is the ventilator, is it?" He pointed to a hole
high up in the wall near the corner of the room, which was
covered with a rusty grating.

"Yes."

"It communicates, as you know, with the other room."

"You would find it very difficult to pass anything up through this
aperture."

"No, I should think it very easy to do so." He approached the
grating, and with the help of his long, thin fingers and his
pocket knife, he raised one of the cross-bars. He then widened
the opening.

"It is a pity that the window is blocked," said he, and let the
cross-bar fall back into place.

"Oh," cried Miss Stoner, "if you are really looking for the
speckled band, you should go to the Indian room."

"Which is this?"

"It is that one." She pointed to the cupboard.

"Let me see," said Holmes, opening it carefully.


Dr. Roylott's chamber was larger than that of his stepdaughters,
but was as plainly furnished. A camp-bed, a small wooden table,
and a couple of chairs constituted all its furniture. There was
a single window looking out upon the lawn, and another looking
into the courtyard. The doctor's clothes were scattered about
the room, and his huge boots lay in the middle of the floor.
Holmes examined with great care the window which looked out upon
the lawn, and then cast an even more careful glance at the one
which faced the yard.

"Now, Miss Stoner," said he, "let us look at the ventilator."

Dr. Roylott's chamber was larger than that of his stepdaughters,
but was as plainly furnished. A camp bed, a small wooden
washstand, a chair, and a table, composed the entire
furnishings. In one corner stood a tall, wooden chest, bound with
iron bands, and studded with copper nails. Holmes immediately
made for this chest, and examined it with minute care. He looked
at the lock, he tried the hinges, he shook it, and he sounded
it. Then he went on to the bed and scrutinized it with the same
care. When he had finished his observations he looked round
at us with a triumphant expression.

"The room is certainly peculiar," he remarked, "but the
peculiarities are such as would naturally appeal to the eye of an
observer. For example, this chest is, I have no doubt, of some
considerable age and the brass nails which are so thickly studded
around it are undoubtedly of the kind which were formerly used by
native workmen in India. Then there is a peculiar smell in the
room, of which I have no doubt that you both are aware--the smell
of the strong Indian cigars which this gentleman is fond of
smoking. Finally, observe this ventilator, which is some two
feet square, and is situated in the upper portion of the room
immediately opposite the large opening for the chimney."

"Oh, I see!" said Miss Stoner, after examining the ventilator
carefully. "There is something very singular indeed about that
opening."

Dr. Roylott's chamber was larger than that of his stepdaughters,
but was as plainly furnished. A heavy, old-fashioned bed and a
washstand were its chief contents; but in one corner stood a
large, bulbous glass chemical safe with a three-legged stool in
front of it. This caught Holmes's attention at once. He approached
it and looked at it with a curious expression upon his face.

"How long has he had that?" he asked.

"Always. It has been there as long as I can remember."

"This is indeed very interesting. It would appear that the doctor
is a man of scientific tastes. Has he ever been known to do any
experiments here?"

"Oh, yes, frequently. Sometimes he would disappear for days into
his laboratory, and would only appear again when his work was
finished."

"What does he do?"

"I don't know. It's some kind of Indian snake-poison, I think."

"Ah, that is most suggestive."

Dr. Roylott's chamber was larger than that of his stepdaughters,
but was as plainly furnished. A camp bed, a small wooden chair,
and a heavy oak chest were its only contents, except for a
narrow, iron safe, which stood in one corner. Holmes, however,
paid little attention to these details. His eyes were fixed upon
a small hole in one of the floor-boards in front of the fireplace.
"This is the ventilation," said he, "and it is surely of an
unusual character. The whole system is singular. What is the
meaning of this aperture? It is quite impossible to see from the
outside."

"I never noticed it before," said Miss Stoner.

"We shall look into it," said Holmes, and he took the poker and
tried to move the board. It resisted all his attempts.

"It must be pretty secure if it can stand that," he muttered.

"This is strange," he said at last, "extraordinary, indeed! I
cannot imagine how a ventilator could be so constructed. This
board is too heavy to have been raised by the hand. It must have
been moved from above. If we are to solve this puzzle, we must
go up to the rooms above."

Dr. Grimesby Roylott's chamber was larger than that of his
step-daughter, but was as plainly furnished. A camp-bed, a small
wooden shelf full of books, mostly of a technical character, an
armchair beside the bed, a plain wooden chair against the wall, a
round table, and a large iron safe were the principal things
which met the eye. Holmes walked slowly round and examined each
and all of them with the keenest interest.

"What's in here?" he asked, tapping the safe.

"My stepfather's business papers."

"Oh! you have seen inside, then?"

"Only once, some years ago. I remember that it was full of
papers."

"There isn't a cat in it, for example?"

"No. What a strange idea!"

"Well, look at this!" He took up a small saucer of milk which
stood on the top of it.

"No; we don't keep a cat. But there is a cheetah and a baboon."

"That is what we call evidence, my dear Watson. And now for the
ventilator."

He looked at it long and earnestly, then examined it with his lens.
Finally he put his finger into the hole and suddenly withdrew it
with a sharp expression of pain.

"Well, I hardly expected that," said he. "It's not quite so
pleasant as it looks. There are some curious gipsies about
here."

"Oh, my heavens, what can it be?" screamed Miss Stoner.

"It's not quite so bad as it seems," said Holmes, though his face
was clearly very grave. "Nevertheless it's not pleasant to be
bitten by a snake. This will have to be placed on the list of
mysterious incidents which surround us."

"A snake!" exclaimed Miss Stoner.

"It is not possible that a snake could come down from the
ventilator?" I asked.

"I suppose it is possible, though it seems a little unlikely,"
Holmes replied.

"But how could it get into your room, Miss Stoner?" I asked.

"I confess that I cannot think," she replied.

"That is what puzzles me," said Holmes. "In the last century,
however, it may have had some more sinister use. However, we shall
leave that until we have examined the other room. I think, now,
that we shall proceed to your sister's room, and see if we can
discover any traces which may help us."

"That is what we have to find out. Everything is pointing to the
fact that there is something very unusual about this room. This
small side-door, which I have no doubt leads to the corridor,
is quite new, it is not fitted with a lock, and the hinges
are attached to the door in such a way that the door can be
opened and closed without any noise, provided that one knew
which way the handle should be turned. The ventilator, too,
leads only into the room. It is clear that there is some
connection between all these facts. The presence of the
bell-rope, and the milk, is, of course, suggestive.

"Yes, I am quite sure that it has to do with the case, but
what is that connection?"

"Why, it is obvious," said Holmes, laughing, "that it must
be some sort of a signal to someone in the next room. You
may remember that your sister told you she had heard a low
whistle before her death. Now we have discovered that a whistle
can be produced in that very room by tying a loop of whipcord
round a small bell. There is no doubt that it is a signal.
But why does she not tell us what that signal meant?"

"I should not have thought of that."

"That's the thing that interests me so much. What was the
significance of that peculiar dying cry—'It was the band! The
speckled band'?"


"That is what puzzles me," said Holmes. "In examining the
ventilator I found this singular fact. The tube, as you perceive,
is lined with a reddish dust. Now, on making a chemical analysis
of this I find that it is composed of a complex poison, known in
India as 'the deadly nightshade.' I found the same reddish dust
upon the bell-pull. In a word, I am convinced that the death of
your sister was caused by some such means as I now suggest. The
tube in which I found this dust passes from Miss Stoner's room to
your stepfather's; so it could very well have been used to convey
the poison into her chamber. The same tube is used for the bell-
pull which she was told to use if she needed assistance. The
poison was only administered once; the only other occasion that
she heard the whistle was when she lay dying, when obviously it
would have been impossible to do anything of the sort. Now, all
this is pretty clear, isn't it?"

"But how could it be done?"

"That is what we shall proceed to find out. A most singular
business! Is that a snake?"

"Good heavens, it's a swamp adder!"

"That is just what I want to know," said Holmes. "It's a detail
that I want to understand. Now for the ventilator."

He went over to the window and examined it with his keen eyes. "It
is connected with the next room," said he. "That is clear enough.
But if I understand rightly, this side is a blind wall, and no
window looks into the room from outside. That is unusual, and it
is certainly a ventilator which could be shut tightly. By
the way, may I ask, Miss Stoner, whether there were any gipsies
in the plantation last night?"

"Yes, quite a number of them."

"Are there gipsies usually in the plantation at this time of
the year?"

"I think that several of them have been there all winter."

"Then it is evidently not so unusual, and that removes a difficulty.
One more question. Did your sister ever receive any mysterious
letters or messages?"

"No."

"You are sure?"

"Oh, yes, quite sure."

"That is very curious," said Holmes. "Well, I think we have got
all we can from this chamber. It is well to use our time to the
best advantage now, and there is some little work that we may do
in the corridor. Might I ask for a little more light?"

"That is not quite so common, is it? Ah, me! it's a wicked world,
and when a clever man turns his brains to crime it is the worst
of all. I think that I have seen enough now, Miss Stoner, and
with your permission we shall walk out upon the lawn."

"Then my friend and I must spend the night in your room, and we
shall see if the mysterious occurrence can be repeated. The
room remains as your sister left it?"

"No, some changes have been made since her death. She had no bell
pull, though she always locked her door."

"How long is it since the bell-pull was put in?"

"About two years ago."

"Very good. Is there anything else in the room at the present
which was not there then?"

"No, nothing."

"Then I think we may lay our plans. We must have some one at
the Crown Inn to give a signal, if anything occurs. Now, let us
return to the house."

"Then, my dear Miss Stoner, we must put a notice in the window to
the effect that your room is occupied by friends who are
inconvenient to be disturbed before a certain hour. We shall
take the precaution of posting an old woman outside the door with
instructions to admit no one. Thus there shall be no possibility
of any interruption. I have also prepared a small supply of
bread and milk for the two of us. We could not bring more than
this, since we were bound to be somewhat secretive, and
unobtrusive in our preparations."

"Do you think there is any real danger?" asked Miss Stoner with
wide eyes.


"I have no doubt that there is. My life is in danger too, Miss
Stoner. And there are very few people indeed in this country who
can afford to lose life, even less, a life such as mine."

"And from those windows the movements of anyone about this house
might be watched?"

"Oh yes, quite easily."

"Then it is settled. We stop there to-night. We shall spend the
night in your room, and we shall place ourselves in communication
with the Crown Inn, so that by means of a telephone we can have
instant information of anything which may occur during the night.
We shall put things in such an order that whatever happens in the
house will be known to us. Now go back to your room and wait for
us. Watson will stay with you. I wish to make a careful survey of
the grounds before it grows dark."

"Then my friend and I must occupy your room to-night. We shall
place ourselves at the window, so that we can see anyone who
approaches your house. You must remain here in your room, and on
no account must you open the door to anyone to-night, unless you
hear me call. Then you may open it with safety. You understand
?"

"Yes."

"It may mean danger to you if you disobey my instructions."

"I am perfectly willing to trust myself in your hands."

"Then there is only one other point. It is of vital importance
that you should leave your room as little as possible tonight,
and especially that you should not under any circumstances
approach the window of your sister's chamber."

"I understand."

"Is there anything else that I should know?"

"Yes, one more thing. You must get to your room as quickly as
possible."

"Why?"

"Because the old man will be back at any moment, and you could
not get out without being seen."

"Then it must be so. We shall spend the night in your room, and
we shall place the lamp there so as to get a good view of what
occurs. Your stepfather, however, may suspect that we are in the
house, and if he finds us there we might find ourselves in a
difficult situation, but with your help we must arrange to keep
him out of our way. Now, I would suggest that we should be in
position by about nine o'clock to-night, and that when we see
that all is quiet we may let you into the room from the outside."

"Yes, but how will we get in?"

"I shall come over the wall from the garden. I will explain
everything in detail when we are at the inn."

"But what will your friend, Mr. Holmes, do?"

"I shall take him along."

"Good heavens! It would be terrible if he were discovered."

"Perhaps it is not advisable to wait for that moment; so without
any further ado we will return to the Crown Inn."

"You must confine yourself to your room, on pretence of a
headache, when your stepfather comes back. Then when you hear him
retire for the night, you must open the shutters of your window,
undo the hasp, put your lamp there as a signal to us, and then
withdraw quietly with everything which you are likely to want
into the room which you used to occupy. I have no doubt that, in
spite of the repairs, you could manage there for one night."

"Oh, yes, easily."

"The rest you will leave in our hands."

"But what will you do?"

"We shall spend the night in your room, and we shall investigate
the cause of this noise which has disturbed you."

"I believe, Mr. Holmes, that you have already made up your mind,"
said Miss Stoner, laying her hand upon my companion's sleeve.

"Perhaps I have."

"Then, for pity's sake, tell me what was the cause of my sister's
death."

"I should prefer to have clearer proofs before I speak."

"You can at least tell me whether my own thought is correct, and
if she died from some sudden fright."

Holmes and I walked down to the Crown Inn, and having ordered our
dinner, we proceeded to enjoy a leisurely conversation concerning
the case which had brought us there. Holmes was exceedingly
cheerful and was full of his usual enthusiasm. He explained his
whole reasoning to me with the utmost lucidity and with an
insistence which would admit of no doubt in my mind of the
correctness of his conclusions.

"To-night," said he, "is our opportunity. It is the night of the
eclipse. When this strange creature, whatever it may be, comes
from its lair it will not be able to distinguish the outlines of
the house, and its usual keenness of perception will be
reduced to zero."

"But what, then, is this creature?"

"A snake, of course."

"A snake? What kind of snake?"

"A peculiar and very poisonous kind."

"What do you mean to do?"

"What does our brave client do to show her gratitude for my
invaluable services?" asked Holmes.

"She will not hurt me, I hope?"

"Not if I can help it."

"No. I mean the lady is ready to reward you at any time. She will
be married, she tells us, in a month's time."

"Ah! this is very important. And what did she say?"

"She said that you should not find her ungrateful when she had
the control of her income. This seems a fair promise to me."

"Yes, but it was a promise made at a moment when she had no
control over her own income, and that is not quite what I
should expect. Then when it comes to the payment you must know
that the lady was prepared to pay us well for our services. She
was prepared to pay us even at this moment, but this is
something which I find a little unusual."

"You do not think that is all right, then?"

"No. This is not all. There are still some other points which I
should like to consider with you."

"All right. Let us discuss those points."

"Thank you. I am glad that we can settle this easily."

"And now, my dear Watson, what is your opinion as to how we shall
spend the time before the night comes?"

"I think that a game of chess would be an excellent idea."

"I think that you are right. Let us go then."

They proceeded to play the game, and in the middle of the game a
messenger brought a message from Miss Stoner that her stepfather
had returned.

"Excellent," said Holmes. "Then we have just enough time to go
there."


Holmes and I left our client at the door, and walked away
together in the direction of the village.  "Now for the Crown
Inn," he remarked, "for a bit of supper and then for bed. Early
to bed and early to rise, Watson, and we shall catch the
speckled band."

Holmes and I walked together to the Crown Inn, and having ordered
our lunch, sat down to discuss the situation.  He was in a
cheerful and expectant mood, for the mystery, which had appealed
to his love of the unusual, seemed to have stimulated him to
extraordinary energy.

Holmes and I walked away together towards the village, and as we
did so he explained his intention. "It is perfectly clear," he
said, "that the death of Miss Stoner's sister was not due to
natural causes, but that some terrible fright or shock had been
the cause of her death. It is equally certain that the cause of
that fright must be something which could only exist in this
room, since it occurred immediately after her sister's
removal. That cause is probably of an unusual nature, since it
must be capable of producing such a violent shock. The bell-rope
and the ventilator are most suggestive, and here it is clear,
from the presence of the milk, that there is something in that
safe which could account for the strange appearance of the
woman's death, and it is worth noting that the milk suggests a
creature which might have some connection with this singular
case."

"But what creature and what cause, Holmes?"

"I cannot answer those questions till after I have made an
examination of the ventilator, and the safe. That is why I
decided that we should spend the night in the room."


Holmes and I walked along the road in silence until we reached
the Crown Inn, which stood facing the park gates. We ordered our
dinner there and, having finished it, went out for a stroll
around the village. The evening was clear, and the first
stars were beginning to appear, but our conversation was
intermittent and we were both preoccupied with our own thoughts.
I noted, however, that my companion looked keenly at every
passer-by, with the result that we met very few people.

"This Roylott is a man who inspires a great fear," I remarked.

"He has certainly an extraordinary influence upon those around
him. He seems to be feared as much by the gipsies as by the
villagers. I am anxious to see whether his character corresponds
with the accounts which we have received."

Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and
sitting-room at the Crown Inn. They were on the upper floor, and
from our window we could command a view of the avenue gate, and
of the inhabited wing of Stoke Moran Manor House. At dusk we saw
Dr. Grimesby Roylott drive past, his huge form looming up beside
the little figure of the lad who drove him. The boy had some
slight difficulty in undoing the heavy iron gates, and we heard
the hoarse roar of the doctor's voice and saw the fury with which
he shook his clinched fists at him. The trap drove on, and a few
minutes later we saw a sudden light spring up among the trees as
the lamp was lit in one of the sitting-rooms.

"Do you know, Watson," said Holmes as we sat together in the
gathering darkness, "I have really some scruples as to taking you
to-night. There is a distinct element of danger."

"Can I be of assistance?"

"Your presence might be invaluable."

"Then I shall certainly come."

"It is very kind of you."

"You speak of danger. You have evidently seen more in these rooms
than was visible to me."

"No, but I fancy that I may have deduced a little more. I imagine
that you saw all that I did."

"I saw nothing remarkable save the bell-rope, and what purpose
that could answer I confess is more than I can imagine."

"You saw the ventilator, too?"

"Yes, but I do not think that it is such a very unusual thing to
have a small opening between two rooms. It was so small that a
rat could hardly pass through."

"I knew that we should find a ventilator before ever we came to
Stoke Moran."

"My dear Holmes!"

"Precisely. The only point which we have to determine is what
that crime is. We must be ready for anything. Now, it is nearly
ten; we must wait another hour before we venture out. I have
already ordered supper to be laid in our room. You have no objection
to two or three slices of cold beef and a pint of beer?"

"None in the world."

"Then let us wait patiently and see what comes of this."

We sat in the window, and looked out into the beautiful night.

The moon shone brightly upon the scene, and the shadows of the
trees lay long and dark upon the ground. The lights from the
windows of Stoke Moran shone out through the trees, and the
dark shape of the house against the clear sky was more distinct
than it had been even by day. As we sat there we heard a
distant whistle. Holmes sprang to his feet, and in an instant he
had torn the blinds from the window and was peering out into the
darkness.

"You have heard that whistle?" he asked.

"Yes, I heard it."

"It was a single note, very low, very sweet, and very
singular."

"It is the same that Miss Stoner heard?"

"Yes, this is a business of importance, Watson."

"Precisely! You saw that small dog whip, the other end of which
was tied into a loop. Now, there is such a thing as a spring
trap, but it is not common as a rule. Yet I fancy that our friend
the doctor is a man who would not hesitate at such a device. What
would you say to a snake, for example?"

"A snake?"

"Yes. A swamp adder, perhaps. Or a cobra. Some creature which
could be trained to do its work among the ventilators."

"Good heavens, Holmes! It's horrible!"

"Quite so. But there is no other explanation, I think, of the
facts. And now, let us get out our pistols and look to our
revolvers. The night promises to be lively."

"Precisely so. The crime is a very subtle one, and would probably
be hushed up if we did not interfere. I have already told you
that the doctor has an interest in preventing his stepdaughter's
marriage. But what has he to do with Miss Julia Stoner's death?
This is a problem which we must solve tonight, and for that
purpose we must leave immediately."

"Precisely so. We are about to witness a most unusual
performance. You will see that I am prepared for every eventuality." He held up a small, flat, tin box from which he took two
powerful electric torches. “These,” said he, “are specially
made for this occasion. We shall need them as soon as it is
dark. Now let us get some rest before our vigil commences.
Remember, we are not to speak or move until I give the order."

"Precisely! You are perfectly right. The doctor is not a man who
cares for the refinements of life. But he has an Eastern
mind, and there is a certain amount of cunning in him. Now let us
look at the matter from another point of view. From the
description of Miss Stoner, this bed was put in the room after
the death of her sister. No doubt it is an ordinary camp-bed.
But let us consider what the doctor did when he found his
stepdaughter was about to marry. Did he give an obvious warning?
No; he employed a more subtle and far-reaching plan. He placed
the girl in the bed in which her sister had died. He removed
all the objects in the room save the rope and the ventilator. And
then at the opportune moment he gave her a message which he knew
would bring her into the room, where he could carry out his
design."

"But what could he intend to do?"

"That, my dear Watson, is just what we are now about to find out."

"Subtle enough and horrible enough. When a doctor does go wrong
he is the first of criminals. He has nerve and he has knowledge.
Palmer and Pritchard were among the heads of their profession.
This man strikes even deeper, but I think, Watson, that we shall
be able to strike deeper still. But we shall have horrors enough
before the night is over; for goodness' sake let us have a quiet
pipe and turn our minds for a few hours to something more
cheerful."

We hastily descended, leaving our small impedimenta in our room.
Taking a dark lantern, Holmes led the way across the grounds, and
through the broken gateway into the courtyard. There was no light
in the central block of buildings, but a single lamp was burning
in the wing which we had visited before. As we approached the
door of the Manor House the heavy beating of a heart was audible
through the stillness.  We had reached the door and Holmes was
about to try it when Miss Stoner appeared at the window, beckoned
to us, and then disappeared.

We waited until the light was extinguished before we ventured out
into the night. Then we stole quietly across the lawn, and into
the shadow of the Manor House. The night was very dark. We
passed along the path in single file, Holmes leading, and I
following with the dog-cart. The air was damp, and had the
pleasant smell of earth and leaves. We had reached the door of
the central block when we heard distinctly the sound of some
heavy object falling within the house. Miss Stoner had given us
the key, and so we were able to enter without difficulty. We did
so, and there we stood within the corridor. A dark passage went
straight before us, and doors lined the sides of it. The air was
hot and heavy, and felt charged with the presence of some
terrible tragedy.

We hurried downstairs and into the street. The night was fine, and
the large moon was shining brilliantly upon the scene. We crossed
the stile and made our way through the fields towards the house.
As we approached it we could hear the sound of some one moving
quickly about the rooms. We passed through the open gate, and into
the grounds. Miss Stoner was waiting for us at the door. She
showed us into her room, where we found that everything had been
prepared as Holmes had directed. We examined the room
carefully, noticing that Miss Stoner had, as desired, moved
everything she would need into the other bedroom. We locked and
bolted both doors and put the lamp on the window as a signal.  Then we settled down to wait.


We hurried across the lawn, through the gap in the hedge, and
found ourselves in the shrubbery which surrounded the house. The
windows of the room were open, and a dark figure could be seen
within.

"That's Miss Stoner," whispered Holmes. "She is now in her former
room, which gives us a clear view of the ventilator."

We waited no longer, but, picking up our sticks and our
revolvers, we stole quietly out of the inn and took the path
which led to the Manor House. It was exceedingly dark, but I could
feel the damp grass beneath my feet, and hear the dull rustling
of the wind amongst the branches. A small side-door in the
rear of the building was open, and through it we passed. Then we
crossed a small yard, and then there was the corridor in which the
three bedrooms lay. The door of the middle room was open. A long
shadow flickered upon the walls, then the door closed suddenly, and
all was dark within.

"Now, Watson," said Holmes, "take a look through that ventilator
and tell me what you see."

I did as he asked, and saw that the window in the next room was
partially open. The lower shutter was halfway up, and the upper
one was closed. I could see that the room was well lit by a
lamp on the table. But as I looked I made a small exclamation.

"What is it?" asked Holmes, turning quickly.

"There is something moving in there."

"Something moving? What is it?"

"There is a dark figure, and it is moving swiftly, up and down,
and about the room."

"The light seems to be flickering. It is going lower, or
else..."

"My God! it's a snake!"

"A snake? Where did it come from?"

"It seems to have come from the ventilator. It is gliding
rapidly."

"This is beyond our investigation now. This is the matter of the
police."

"I do not think so. It is our duty now to follow the snake."

As we passed out he exchanged a few words with the landlord,
explaining that we were going on a late visit to an acquaintance,
and that it was possible that we might spend the night there. A
moment later we were out on the dark road, a chill wind blowing
in our faces, and one yellow light twinkling in front of us
through the gloom to guide us on our sombre errand.

We ascended the steps, and Holmes, with his key, opened the door.
We entered the passage and went straight to Miss Stoner's room. The
light was still there, and Miss Stoner herself was standing
by the window, dressed in her outdoor clothes, her face ashen
white, and her hands tightly clasped together.

"I have done as you told me," she said.

"Good," replied Holmes. "Now we shall proceed to fulfill our
part. Take Miss Stoner to your own room, Watson. But remain
outside the door, and not enter until I call. Keep your eyes open,
and if you see anything unusual, you will notify me. Above all,
no noise. Remember that our investigation is far from being over,
and it would be a pity to have to take any more unpleasantness at
this juncture. I wish you to watch very carefully while I try to
bring the case to a swift conclusion."

We entered the window, the light still shining brightly from the
table. Miss Stoner was waiting for us, her face pale but her
eyes resolute. She had already packed a small bag with a few
necessary things. We carried them down to her former room and
made her as comfortable as possible. Holmes then examined the
room, and the shutter of the ventilator with a lens and a hammer.

"The other room is entirely empty," she whispered.

"No, it is not," said Holmes. "There is a ventilator which
communicates with it, and there is some curious machinery in
this." He put his hand over the ventilator and spoke through it
in a voice which was hardly audible.

"There is no response. I am speaking to the lady who was
sleeping in the next room. If you are awake, please reply."

There was no answer.

"You may possibly be able to see more easily," he continued. "I
think that you must feel how thin these walls are. Please
examine carefully the condition of the woodwork."

"You will get accustomed to the dark, and you will see what
I mean. Look carefully."

"There is nothing."

"Look at the hole, too."

"I still see nothing."

"Please look again, carefully."

"Surely there must be something there. I see a snake?"

"Yes, that is it. A very large and venomous snake."


We entered the room, and as Miss Stoner had arranged, the lamp
was set upon the table. Holmes instantly struck a match and lit
the gas. The only other light came from the window, which was
partially open. In the centre of the room, lying on its back,
was the unfortunate Miss Stoner. Her eyes were closed, and her face
was as white as death. For a moment I thought that she was dead,
but as I bent over her I saw that she was alive. The whole of her
body was convulsed with agony, her limbs were stiff, and her hands
were clenched into fists. She was as rigid as a corpse.

"This is a case for the physician, Watson," said Holmes,
drawing his little case from his pocket. "It's evidently
something of the nature of a poison or a fit. There is nothing
unusual about her pulse, though I admit she is perfectly rigid.
No, thank you, Miss Stoner, no; I would prefer that you kept
yourself quiet and undisturbed for a few minutes. I'm only going
to do what is necessary to help her."

He opened the little case and examined the contents carefully,
laying them out beside the lamp. Then he produced a tiny bottle
from his case, and with a small glass dropper proceeded to
administer a few drops to the rigid woman. She swallowed it and
then lay back with her eyes shut in a more natural position, her
body beginning to relax in a few moments. 


We entered the room, and at once Miss Stoner's lamp was placed
upon the table. The shutters were closed, and we were left in
darkness save for the glow from our own lights. Miss Stoner had
brought with her a small dressing-case and some articles of
clothing. With the help of a dark lantern I examined the room,
while Holmes gave his attention to the ventilator. This was the
only point of interest, and there was no sign of the noise which
had so greatly disturbed Miss Stoner. With the aid of our
lanterns we examined the room carefully, Miss Stoner herself
pointing out the bed which her sister had occupied. As she did so,
I observed a peculiar expression upon her face.

"I think that there is no doubt," said Holmes, "that the ventilator
is the only real opening into this room."

"Oh! my God!" cried Miss Stoner; "I see the thing now!"

"Well?" I said as Holmes examined her face anxiously.

"Is this a bed?" she screamed. "It's a coil of rope!"

"Yes, a curious kind of bed," said Holmes, "a very curious kind
of bed."

We entered the window, and found Miss Stoner waiting for us
inside. She was dressed in her warmest clothes, and had a small
bag with her.  "I was so anxious," she said, "to have your
protection that I would not rest until I had made some excuse to
get away from him."  

"Good," said Holmes, "now, Miss Stoner, if you will lead the way,
we shall go quietly into the other room and await developments."

I had forgotten the strange pets which the doctor affected. There
was a cheetah, too; perhaps we might find it upon our shoulders
at any moment. I confess that I felt easier in my mind when,
after following Holmes' example and slipping off my shoes, I
found myself inside the bedroom. My companion noiselessly closed
the shutters, moved the lamp onto the table, and cast his eyes
round the room. All was as we had seen it in the daytime. Then
creeping up to me and making a trumpet of his hand, he whispered
into my ear again so gently that it was all that I could do to
distinguish the words:

"The least sound would be fatal to our plans."

I nodded to show that I had heard.

"We must sit without light. He would see it through the
ventilator."

I nodded again.

"Do not go asleep; your very life may depend upon it. Have your
pistol ready in case we should need it. I will sit on the side of
the bed, and you in that chair."

I took out my revolver and laid it on the corner of the table.

How long we sat there I cannot tell. It felt like hours, though it
may have been but a little time. The darkness was thick enough
to be felt; and it was only by the occasional turning of the
lamp that we could satisfy ourselves that we were not utterly
alone in the room.  Then, suddenly, there came a low whistle from
the next room, followed by a distinct metallic clang, as if some
heavy body had fallen on the stone flooring.

How long it was before I dozed I cannot tell. I was awakened by
a sudden scratching sound, a sort of grating that seemed to come
from the ventilator. I looked round, and there was Holmes sitting
upright, listening intently. A moment later the scratching came
again, and then there was a distinct click. Holmes struck a
match, and held it to the ventilator.

How long we sat there I cannot tell. It seemed to me that we
must have been in that room for hours, but Holmes, by his watch,
asserted that it was not more than an hour and a quarter. It
became clear to me that every sound which we could possibly hear
during that period came from outside, and the room seemed to be
absolutely quiet.  At last, however, a low, distinct whistle
reached my ears.

How long it was before I slept I cannot tell. I was conscious of
the intense stillness of the room and the presence of my
companion, and I had also a vague impression of the gentle
swinging to and fro of the lamp. Then my eyes closed and I
dropped into a most profound sleep.  I was awakened by a sharp
click. Holmes had sprung up from the bed.

"I hear a distinct noise," he whispered. "A low whistle, and a
metallic scraping sound."

I sat up and strained my ears.

"Yes, I hear it, too."

"It is on the other side of the wall. It seems to me that it is
coming from the ventilator."

"What can it be?"

"Keep quiet. It is a curious thing, but I believe I have seen
enough of the mystery to get us started."

How long we sat I cannot tell. It seemed to me that we had been
there for hours, when I suddenly felt a touch upon my shoulder.
Holmes' voice whispered in my ear:

"Keep perfectly still. He is coming."

I felt a cold hand touch my own. I saw a dark form, that of a
man, gliding along from the ventilator towards the bed. It was
followed by a second form, and I realised with a shock of horror
that the second form was that of a large snake.

How shall I ever forget that dreadful vigil? I could not hear a
sound, not even the drawing of a breath, and yet I knew that my
companion sat open-eyed, within a few feet of me, in the same
state of nervous tension in which I was myself. The shutters cut
off the least ray of light, and we waited in absolute darkness.

It was just after three that I suddenly heard a sound so
extraordinary that it sent a chill of horror to my heart. It was
a low, clear whistle, such as my sister described, and then,
following it, a prolonged, metallic scraping, as of some hard
substance moving slowly across a wooden floor.

It was just after three that I suddenly heard a low clear whistle
from the centre of the room. I knew that it was the same
whistle which had been described to me. I sprang up in my chair,
when, at the same instant, there was a wild scream from
outside, and a long drawn sigh, which was followed by the heavy
fall of a body upon the floor.

It was just after three that a low whistle, drawn through the
teeth, was heard outside the window. It was such a sound as
might have been made by some one calling to a dog. I felt Holmes
grip my wrist, and he rose softly to his feet. I followed his
example, and we stood together, listening intently. The sound
came again -- a low sibilant note. Then I heard a distinct scraping
sound, and the gentle rattling of a chain.

It was just after three that I felt a sudden change in the
atmosphere of the room, something like the approach of a breeze,
but there was no draught to account for it. Then I heard a noise
which I can only describe as a low, humming sound, like that of a
great engine working at high pressure. It grew louder and louder
until it seemed that the whole house would vibrate with it. I
could feel the blood leaving my face, for I knew that it was the
approach of something deadly.

At last, a low, clear whistle drifted up from the ground below.
I sprang to my feet, but Holmes's hand was on my arm and I sat
down again. The whistle was repeated, and then a long, thin,
metallic clang, as though a bar of iron had been thrown down
upon a stone floor.

"That was the signal," whispered Holmes. "It is time for us to
start."

He struck a match and examined the ventilator. The wooden
shutter was quite in place. Then he lit the candle and examined
the bell-rope. There was nothing unusual there.

Suddenly there was the momentary gleam of a light up in the
direction of the ventilator, which vanished immediately, but was
succeeded by a strong smell of burning oil and heated metal.
Someone in the next room had lit a dark-lantern. I heard a gentle
sound of movement, and then all was silent once more, though the
smell grew stronger. For half an hour I sat with straining ears.
Then suddenly another sound became audible--a very gentle,
soothing sound, like that of a small jet of steam escaping
continually from a kettle. The instant that we heard it, Holmes
sprang from the bed, struck a match, and lashed furiously with
his cane at the bell-pull.

"You see it, Watson?" he yelled. "You see it?"

The door between the two rooms was slightly ajar, so that a
chink of light came through, and showed that a candle was lit
within. Holmes pushed it open, and we entered. Dr. Grimesby
Roylott was lying dead upon his face. His face was a picture of
agonized terror, and his limbs were terribly distorted. The
cheetah, the baboon, and the Indian snake were still in their
cages, but the doctor’s face and neck were horribly swollen, the
eyes bulging and starting from their sockets and the skin showing
a purplish colour. It was evident that he had died in some
violent agony. The candle on the table was not burned out, and the
match which had been used was still on the carpet, but there were
no other traces of violence. We searched, however, without
success.

"There is nothing here," said Holmes; "but a careful examination
of the ventilator might show us something."

"What do you expect to find?"

"Some clue as to how the poison was administered."

"But what poison could produce such symptoms?"

"There is only one drug known to the pharmacopoeia, which is
capable of producing such symptoms and that is the Indian swamp
adder. I got the details of its poisonous properties from
old books during my visit to Doctors' Commons."

The door between the two rooms was slightly ajar. We pushed it
open and entered. A most singular spectacle met our eyes. On the
floor lay the gigantic frame of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, his face
as white as chalk, his eyes staring wildly up at the ceiling. He
was clad in his dressing-gown, and his limbs were drawn up
towards his body in the attitude of a man who has died in great
agony. Beside him lay a cruel-looking, rusty old muzzle-loading
pistol, and close to this was a peculiar serpentine object which
at first I took to be a particularly large snake. It was,
however, a richly coloured band or scarf of some kind, and, as I
picked it up, I observed that it was made of a curious thin,
black material, interwoven with something that looked like
yellow flowers. There was nothing else of interest in the room.

"There's the case," said Holmes, pointing to the dead body. "There
are our proofs."

"And the speckled band?"

"Precisely so. A tropical snake of a venomous character. The
marks on my client's wrist were such as might have been made by
the grip of a large snake. And if you remember the death of Miss
Stoner was shrouded in mystery. The marks of the creature on her
wrist could only be seen by careful examination of the body. The
coroner was, of course, utterly baffled, as was the local
surgeon. The only clue was that it was a small snake, a point on
which, however, they were never perfectly agreed. Now, you see,
there is no difficulty in solving the mystery. The facts were
there, but the significance of them had to be discovered."

"What was the snake?"

"A swamp adder, of which some specimens have been found in Surrey.
It is no bigger than a whip, but it carries poison, enough to kill
ten men. Its bite is deadly, but it is very sluggish, and averse
to attack."

"What happened then?"

The door between the two rooms was slightly ajar, so that a
light from the corridor streamed into the doctor's chamber.  We
entered, and I instantly saw what the sudden outcry meant.  A
ghastly spectacle met our eyes.  On the table lay a dark lantern,
with a small tube of thick glass projecting from the top.  This
tube was connected to another tube which passed through a hole in
the wall and disappeared into the next room.  On the floor lay a
dead man, clad in a dressing-gown.  The face was contorted, the
eyes staring wildly, and the whole expression of the dead face one
of horror and loathing.  The baboon, which had escaped from its
cage, was perched upon his head, while the cheetah lay upon his
chest, apparently engaged in feeding upon some portion of its
master.

The door was open, and through it we could see that the room was
empty. A table was overturned, and a chair lay broken on the
floor. In the corner was a dark-lantern with a bent hinge. Holmes
picked it up and examined it carefully.

"This is not our visitor's," he remarked. "It is smaller and
older. There is one other point, however, which will be of use to
us." He held up the dog-whip, which he had retrieved from the
stepdaughter's room. "It is of some rare Indian manufacture.
Would anyone here recognize it?"

"The gipsies, perhaps," I suggested.

"Yes, the gipsies, or some one who had traveled in India," said
Holmes. "Now, I think that you will have no difficulty in
understanding the sequence of events. The bed-room is on the
ground floor. The window is open. Dr. Grimesby Roylott has retired
to his room. Miss Stoner, you will remember, looks from her
window and sees Dr. Grimesby Roylott pass in front of the house.
She also smells the odor of his Indian cigar, thus confirming her
suspicion that he is close by. The ventilator is open to his room.
The sound of the steam jet and the whistle indicate that some
form of animal is about to be released from a cage or container.
The animal then travels through the ventilator."

The door between the two rooms was shut, but unlocked. We pushed
it open and entered. A most ghastly spectacle met our eyes. Lying
on his back, with his legs drawn up and his hands clutching at
his throat, was the unfortunate doctor. His face was purple, his
eyes bulging, his tongue protruding. The lamp lay shattered upon
the floor, the dark lantern was close to his hand, and near it was
a little bottle, half full of a dark, reddish liquid, and bearing
the label "Acidum sulfuricum". It is well that he had not
succeeded in his design. There was little doubt as to what had
happened. He had been about to administer a deadly draught to Miss
Stoner, when a cry from the corridor had caused him to turn,
and at that moment the cheetah had sprung upon him. It was
apparent that the creature had inflicted a savage bite upon his
throat. He had defended himself with his lamp, which lay
shattered into a thousand pieces upon the floor. But the sudden
and complete surprise, the savage assault of a beast more than
human in its ferocity, had completely overwhelmed him. In his
struggle he had overturned the small table, and in falling had
smashed the lamp and knocked down the dark lantern which lay now
beside him.

"This, then, is the end of Dr. Grimesby Roylott," said Holmes,
and his face was now as pale as death.

With a grave face he lit the lamp and led the way down the
corridor. Twice he struck at the chamber door without any reply
from within. Then he turned the handle and entered, I at his
heels, with the cocked pistol in my hand.

Its head was black, its eyes were like coals of fire, its mouth
was wide, its tongue was out, and it swayed and hissed, darting
its head to and fro with venomous menace. Holmes had instantly
thrown himself on one side, while I, with a cry of horror, had
leaped to my feet. The reptile had turned upon its master. Its
fangs had met in his hand, and he had writhed and shrieked and
fallen. When we had recovered our senses we examined the body
more closely. There was no sign of any violence other than the
two small puncture marks which we had already seen.

"A death most singular, most curious, most improbable," said Holmes.
"We have all been outwitted."

"Outwitted?" I cried, for the scene was still so strange to me.

"It is not a question of outwitting. It is a question of
deliberate and cunning murder. You had only the bare facts of the
case, and could not possibly know all the circumstances that
pointed to the true culprit."

It was a terrible spectacle. The reptile was of a monstrous size,
fully five feet in length, a venomous swamp adder. Its head was
broad, flat, and triangular, its eyes were large and yellow, and
its skin was of a dusky greenish brown with darker, yellowish
speckles. Holmes had already seized his cane, and as the reptile
protruded its head I saw him drive it down with a frightful
force upon its neck. The creature writhed, and twisted, and
shrieked as Holmes dashed it to the ground. Then with a dart and
a flash it disappeared down the ventilator.

"Thank goodness that's over!" cried Miss Stoner, who had
followed us into the room.

"It is over, indeed, Miss Stoner," said Holmes, gazing at
her with an expression of profound pity. "But it would have been
better that it had been over an hour ago. The creature was
probably half-stifled before it fell. But you see, Miss
Stoner, that its bite was not the cause of death."

"I see nothing," said Miss Stoner, who was beginning to
tremble violently. "But this is the same as the speckled band
that caused my sister's death? Is this why you came here?"


Its eyes shone with a deadly light, its head was distended, and
its tongue flickered out like a forked flame. Then with a
horrible hissing sound it launched itself from its perch and
fell upon the doctor's bare breast. He uttered a scream, and
threw up his hands to beat off the reptile, but it was too late.
As with a whip the snake lashed around him and then, with a
sudden twist of its neck, broke loose and left him there with a
single tiny crimson speck upon his breast.

It was a swamp adder, the deadliest snake in India. Its head was
swollen, and its dull eyes were fixed upon us. The fangs were
deep in his neck. He was already dead. It had struck once and
for ever.

It was a swamp adder, the deadliest of all snakes, its head
raised, its капюшон expanded, its eyes gleaming with a deadly
malice. It struck furiously at the lamp, and then, with a
coiled lash, fell upon its master's head. He gave a cry of
terror, clutching at the creature which was now fastened upon
his throat. Then with a frightful convulsion, the whole thing
collapsed upon the floor, a dead serpent and a lifeless man.

"It is a swamp adder!" cried Holmes; "the deadliest snake in
India. He has died within ten seconds of being bitten. Violence
does, in truth, recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls
into the pit which he digs for another. Let us thrust this
creature back into its den, and we can then remove Miss Stoner to
some place of shelter and let the county police know what has
happened."

We carried out Miss Stoner from her room, and as the dawn broke we
found ourselves at the door of the Manor House, where we met
Inspector Gregory and Sergeant Wilson, who had been summoned by
our telegram.  They were naturally amazed to find us there in
possession, but Holmes' explanation of the case, supported as it
was by the facts and by the condition of the unfortunate
Roylott, soon convinced them.

We then examined more closely the peculiar yellow band which
surrounded the doctor's brow. It was of speckled Indian
rubber, and was clearly fastened by a clasp behind. We found
that it contained a quantity of the same yellow powder which we
had seen used at the bedside of the dying woman. In this way we
had at last obtained the direct proof of the crime which we had
long suspected. The snake, as we had surmised, had escaped from
the safe, and had entered the room through the ventilator,
guided possibly by the smell of the food which was left outside
for the creature's nourishment. The adder had then glided down
from the ventilator, and had fastened upon its victim during the
night.

We then examined more minutely the body of our unfortunate
victim. It was clear that he had been struck by some sudden
terror, which had killed him before he could move. The yellow
band round his brow was an old and familiar Indian device.
Some months before, the doctor had sent for a large supply of
Indian jungle snakes, and these had all escaped from him about the
same time. One of them, the deadliest of all, had evidently
crept back into the house, and had made its way through the
ventilator into the bedroom of Miss Helen Stoner's sister, where
it had done its deadly work. Its further progress had then been
stopped by the fastening of the bed to the floor. It had lived in
the walls during the interval, and had eventually crept into
Dr. Roylott's room, where, disturbed by some noise in the next
apartment, it had struck its fatal blow.

Then we turned our attention to the unfortunate victim. There was
a strong smell of bitter almonds about him. His face was a
curious mixture of anger and fear, with the dark blotches upon
his brow which showed that his death had been a sudden one. His
right hand, clad in a yellow-stained glove, was raised, and he
held something between his finger and thumb. We moved closer and
saw that it was a small, beautifully wrought silver case.

"It looks like a lady's cigarette case," said I.

"A very pretty one, too. Let us see what is inside."

He opened it gently, and out from the silken lining there
sprang a tiny, beautifully spotted lizard.

"A speckled band!" said Holmes, laughing.  "A venomous
species, no doubt, but not deadly. He merely used it to frighten
the ladies."

We then left the room, and as we descended the stairs we met
Miss Stoner, who had been sent for and had come down to see what
was going on. She had heard the cries of her stepfather, but
she had been too terrified to venture near him. As soon as she
understood the true state of affairs she wept with relief, and it
was some time before she was able to control herself.
Such are the true facts of the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, of
Stoke Moran. It is not necessary that I should prolong a
narrative which has already run to too great a length by telling
how we broke the sad news to the terrified girl, how we conveyed
her by the morning train to the care of her good aunt at Harrow,
of how the slow process of official inquiry came to the
conclusion that the doctor met his fate while indiscreetly
playing with a dangerous pet. The little which I had yet to learn
of the case was told me by Sherlock Holmes as we travelled back
next day.

I examined the ventilator, and having, by the aid of my lens,
discovered that the little opening was made in the exact centre
of the partition, I felt that I had solved the mystery. The snake
would crawl through the aperture into the room, and then would
return through the ventilator, after having done its deadly work.
With the aid of Miss Stoner I made a careful examination of the
room.  Our search was rewarded. We found near the ventilator a
small box made of sandalwood, such as is used by the natives of
India for storing jewels. It was sealed with a peculiar
oriental seal, and contained the enormous Indian swamp adder."

I saw the whole thing as clear as day, after this explanation.
The peculiar spots on the handkerchief, the whistle, the
metallic clang, the very peculiar words of the dying woman, all
pointed to the same conclusion.  But what a fool I was not to
have grasped it before!"

I examined the ventilator, and I found, adhering to it, a
number of small scales of a reptile. These I secured, and taking
them to my friend, Mr. Percy Armitage, the naturalist, I found
that they were the scales of a species of amphisbaena--the
speckled band--the deadliest of all venomous snakes, which
makes its nest in loose earth, and is consequently rare in
England. Now, I have only to add a few details. The snake, you
will remember, came through the ventilator at night, and I
expected it to emerge from the same hole. I found, however,
that it came through a new ventilator which had been very cleverly
cut into the wall, directly behind the bed, the tube which passed
through the wall being so narrow that only the snake itself could
pass through, and then only when drawn through from the other
end. It thus appeared that the snake was made to bite the
unfortunate Helen Stoner just as her sister had been bitten before
her, but that the same result did not ensue, because the doctor's
attention was diverted by the presence of Helen Stoner, and he
therefore was obliged to retreat with his deadly weapon, which was
only discovered when I blew the light on it, and so precipitated
its return to the place from whence it came."

"I examined the room very carefully for traces of the creature,
and I found it eventually in the ventilator, and from thence I
deduced that the method of introducing it was through the hole in
the wall, which was also used for the purpose of the ventilator.
The snake had evidently been there some time, for I found a
considerable amount of dust which had gathered upon it. It had
been supplied with milk in a saucer, as I have already mentioned
to you, and so I came to the conclusion that it had been there
for some little time, and that it was the intention of the doctor
to use it upon his stepdaughter. I could not understand why he
should wish to kill his stepdaughter rather than his
step-daughter's suitor. However, I have now seen the will, and I
have no doubt as to what the motive is."

"I admit that I was very nearly beaten, but the speckled band
saved me. I had been watching the lamp—and I saw it suddenly
put out. Then I looked at the ventilator, and saw a dark form
crawling out of it. I instantly lit the lamp and fired a shot.
It was the only chance, for even had I had my revolver in my hand
I could not have fired fast enough to have prevented the reptile
from inflicting a fatal blow. I saw it writhe in the glare of the
lamp, and then I struck at it with the cane. It fell, and it is
now in the safe. The whole thing is so clear to me now that I
cannot imagine how I could have failed to grasp it before."

"I had come to these conclusions before ever I had entered his
room. An inspection of his chair showed me that he had been in
the habit of standing on it, which of course would be necessary
in order that he should reach the ventilator. The sight of the
safe, the saucer of milk, and the loop of whipcord were enough to
finally dispel any doubts which may have remained. The metallic
clang heard by Miss Stoner was obviously caused by her stepfather
hastily closing the door of his safe upon its terrible occupant.
Having once made up my mind, you know the steps which I took in
order to put the matter to the proof. I heard the creature hiss
as I have no doubt that you did also, and I instantly lit the
light and attacked it."

"With the result of driving it through the ventilator."
